analysis:
All changes are in CI test scripts for the threat-review scanner: .github/scripts/test-threat-diagnostics.py (plan_calls assertion on lines 186-187 and 196), test-threat-integration-scope.py (new DepthPolicyTests, lines 63-199, plus a reply hook in Responses) and test-threat-model-review.py (workflow assertions around lines 743-761). No provider, coordinator, attestation, key-handling or cache code is touched, so the provider-side threats (T-041, the T-0xx entries, TB-002/003/007/011) are unaffected.

The tests are offline: they use synthetic responders with no credentials, network access or paid calls. The diagnostics tests continue to assert that private strings never appear in diagnostics output.

The workflow-contract test changes tighten the expected workflow configuration. THREAT_REVIEW_BASE_SHA must come only from github.event.pull_request.base.sha, with no env fallback, which fits the immutable-base-revision model. workflow_dispatch, pr_number and review_depth inputs must be absent from the review job, which removes PR-selectable or manual-trigger paths. A Bedrock workload-call cap (500) and a max-output-tokens cap (16384) are asserted, and the timeout is raised to 60 minutes with a 3000-second scanner limit. This is a CI availability and cost-control posture change, not a security regression. The tests only check the workflow text; the actual workflow file and the scanner modules (threat_review.budget_scan, merge_policy, context) were not supplied. Whether the depth-escalation policy matches what the tests assert, for example critical-path routing to SOL and support-file handling that can still yield a clean verdict, is therefore unverified here. The test_clean_support_files case lets docs and test files skip escalation but keeps SONNET coverage and uncertainty escalation, so I found no concrete weakness. A later pass should check the implementation of the filename classification, such as the workflow-named-as-test case, if those source files are in scope.
